title: Worn clothes
hook: as a person casts off worn clothes, the self casts off worn bodies

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was jisei, a farewell poem. Your line was a traveler's dream crossing it. Today, a turn from Buddhist voices to a Hindu one.

A shirt with a frayed collar and thin elbows, worn so long it's soft as paper. Sooner or later it gets folded and let go. The Bhagavad Gita, a Hindu scripture spoken on a battlefield, reaches for exactly that picture when it talks about death. Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna that the self sets aside worn-out bodies the way a person sets aside worn-out clothes. And he says it to a man standing between two armies.
screen: `A FRAYED SHIRT.` → `SPOKEN ON A BATTLEFIELD.` → `CLOTHES AND THE ONE WHO WEARS THEM.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. Arjuna looks across the field and sees teachers and relatives in the other army. He puts down his bow, grieving before a single arrow has flown. Krishna, his charioteer, whom many Hindus worship as God, begins to answer him. Second, the self. Krishna says the self is never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is slain. A little later he adds that weapons do not cut it and fire does not burn it. Third, the clothes. Between those two teachings comes the picture. In Edwin Arnold's old English verse: "So putteth by the spirit / Lightly its garb of flesh." Clothes wear thin; the one who wears them goes on. It's a household image for one of the hardest questions people ask. Fourth, how it's read. Some Hindu teachers read the verse as comfort, and as a teaching about what in a person lasts. But notice who hears it first: not a mourner at a funeral, a man about to act. Krishna's point, in the poem, is that grief for bodies should not keep Arjuna from his duty. Some readers take the battlefield as a real war; others read it as a picture of the struggle inside a person. Both hear the same verse about clothes. And the week, looking back: death recalled with each breath, the charnel ground, strive on, no one to blame, rebirth, a last poem, and now worn clothes.
screen: `ARJUNA PUTS DOWN HIS BOW.` · `NEVER BORN, NEVER DIES.` · `A GARB OF FLESH, SET ASIDE.` · `SAID TO A MAN ABOUT TO ACT.` · then, large: `WORN CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: If there's an old piece of clothing nearby, take it in your hands; if not, rest a hand on your sleeve. Fold it slowly, noticing the worn places, a thin spot, a loose thread, a softness that only comes from use, and breathe while you fold. You don't have to think about death at all; just handle something worn, gently, and set it down.
Worn clothes: the Bhagavad Gita's picture of the self setting aside a worn body the way a person sets aside worn clothing. Today's word.
Your line: garb of flesh. Set aside lightly, in Arnold's old verse. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita at home, in temples and in study groups, and verses from its second chapter, including this one, are sometimes recited in times of death and grief.

chat.says: Why does the Gita compare death to changing clothes?

It means the body matters most, so care for it like your best clothes.
It's a funeral custom: mourners change clothes to show grief has ended.
